topic_tag: river beetle colony after a flood
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: After surveying the bar in July, one ecologist reported that the year's flood had ______ the colony.

worlds.passage: Each spring flightless beetles nest on a gravel bar in a western river, eating the seeds of low plants there and walking across a narrow gravel spit to mate with colonies on the bank. This year the flood crested no higher than usual and fell within two days, and it left deep, fast water where the spit had been. In July the nests held the usual number of well-fed adults, and not one bank beetle was among them. After surveying the bar in July, one ecologist reported that the year's flood had ______ the colony.
worlds.explanation: Deep water now runs where the spit was, and no bank beetles reached the bar, so the colony is cut off from its mates: the flood "stranded" it. "Sheltered" fails because the only change is a loss, not protection; "starved" fails because the adults were well fed; "swamped" fails because an ordinary flood left the usual number of adults in the nests.

sheltered.quote: not one bank beetle was among them
sheltered.why: The flood cut the colony off from its breeding partners, a loss; it kept no threat away.

starved.why: Well-fed adults were not deprived of food.

swamped.why: An ordinary crest that left the usual number of adults did not overwhelm the nests.

worlds.passage: Each spring flightless beetles nest on a gravel bar in a western river, eating the seeds of low plants there and walking across a narrow gravel spit to mate with colonies on the bank. This year the flood crested no higher than usual, and the spit came back. The water filled the burrows of the bank ants that cross the spit each summer to carry off larvae, no ants reached the bar all season, and in July it held more young than in any year of the survey. After surveying the bar in July, one ecologist reported that the year's flood had ______ the colony.
worlds.explanation: The flood drowned out the ants that raid the larvae, and the colony then raised a record number of young, so the flood protected it: it "sheltered" the colony. "Stranded" fails because the spit came back; "starved" fails because a colony raising record numbers was not short of food; "swamped" fails because an ordinary crest left the colony thriving.

stranded.why: The route to the bank returned, so the colony was not cut off.

starved.quote: more young than in any year
starved.why: A record crop of young means food was not lacking.

swamped.why: An ordinary crest that left the colony thriving did not overwhelm it.

worlds.passage: Each spring flightless beetles nest on a gravel bar in a western river, eating the seeds of low plants there and walking across a narrow gravel spit to mate with colonies on the bank. This year the flood crested no higher than usual, and the spit came back. Its fast water stripped the bar and the bank alike of the low plants, which did not sprout again before autumn, and in July the dry, undisturbed nests held a few thin adults and no larvae. After surveying the bar in July, one ecologist reported that the year's flood had ______ the colony.
worlds.explanation: The flood removed the seed plants on the bar and the bank, and the survivors were thin with no young, so the beetles had nothing to eat: it "starved" the colony. "Stranded" fails because the spit came back; "sheltered" fails because the colony was left with a few thin adults; "swamped" fails because the dry, undisturbed nests.

stranded.why: The route to the bank returned, so the colony was not cut off; the bank had no food either.

sheltered.quote: a few thin adults and no larvae
sheltered.why: A colony reduced to a few thin adults was harmed, not protected.

swamped.why: Dry nests were not overwhelmed by water.

worlds.passage: Each spring flightless beetles nest on a gravel bar in a western river, eating the seeds of low plants there and walking across a narrow gravel spit to mate with colonies on the bank. This year the flood crested higher than any on record and stayed up for three days; the deep-rooted plants stood again once it fell, and the spit came back. In July the burrows were packed with silt, and the bar held only the few adults that had been feeding on the bank when the river rose. After surveying the bar in July, one ecologist reported that the year's flood had ______ the colony.
worlds.explanation: A record crest stood over the bar for days, filled the burrows with silt, and left only beetles that had been off the bar: the flood "swamped" the colony. "Stranded" fails because the spit came back; "starved" fails because the plants stood again at once; "sheltered" fails because only a few adults survived.

stranded.why: The route to the bank returned, so the colony was not cut off.

starved.why: The food plants survived, so hunger was not the effect.

sheltered.why: A colony reduced to the few beetles who happened to be away was harmed, not protected.

topic_tag: lava flow and a valley river
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Mapping the valley today, geologists conclude that the lava ______ the river.

worlds.passage: About nine thousand years ago, a tongue of lava poured into a narrow mountain valley and hardened across the floor where a river had wound in wide loops toward a lake. As it cooled, the lava split along a single crack that runs as true as a surveyor's line for four miles down the middle of the flow. The river found that crack and cut its trench into it, and fish from the lake still swim up the trench each spring to spawn where the river leaves the hills. Mapping the valley today, geologists conclude that the lava ______ the river.
worlds.explanation: The river now follows a crack that runs as true as a surveyor's line for four miles, where it once wound in wide loops: the lava "straightened" it. "Swallowed" fails because the river cut an open trench; "trapped" fails because fish still swim up from the lake, so the river still flows into it; "sidetracked" fails because it still reaches the same lake.

swallowed.why: A river running in an open trench has not disappeared into the rock.

trapped.quote: fish from the lake still swim up the trench
trapped.why: The river still connects to the lake, so it is not held back.

sidetracked.why: The river still feeds its old lake, so it was not diverted elsewhere.

worlds.passage: About nine thousand years ago, a tongue of lava poured into a narrow mountain valley and hardened across the floor where a river had wound in wide loops toward a lake. The lava cooled into rock riddled with hollow tubes, and the old channel across the top of the flow is dry gravel for six miles. At the far end of the flow, springs gush from its base at about the river's old volume, and from there the water winds on to the same lake by its old route. Mapping the valley today, geologists conclude that the lava ______ the river.
worlds.explanation: The channel over the flow is dry, yet the river's full volume gushes out at the far end, so the water runs through the hollow rock underground: the lava "swallowed" it. "Straightened" fails because no channel runs across the flow; "trapped" fails because the whole volume comes out again; "sidetracked" fails because the water reaches the same lake by its old route.

straightened.why: No river runs on the surface of the flow, so it has no new straight course there.

trapped.quote: springs gush from its base at about the river's old volume
trapped.why: The water passes through, so it is not held back.

sidetracked.quote: same lake by its old route
sidetracked.why: The water keeps its old destination, so it was not diverted.

worlds.passage: About nine thousand years ago, a tongue of lava poured into a narrow mountain valley and hardened across the floor where a river had wound in wide loops toward a lake. The lava cooled into dense rock without cracks and banked against both valley walls well above the old riverbed. The water behind it rises in wet decades and sinks back in dry ones, never reaching the lowest notch in the hardened rim, and below the flow the old channel to the lake is dry and grown over with pines. Mapping the valley today, geologists conclude that the lava ______ the river.
worlds.explanation: The water piles up behind a crackless wall it never tops, and nothing reaches the old channel below: the lava "trapped" the river. "Straightened" fails because the river no longer flows on; "swallowed" fails because dense rock without cracks lets no water sink in; "sidetracked" fails because the water never reaches the notch that could carry it away.

straightened.quote: old channel to the lake is dry
straightened.why: A river that no longer flows on has no straightened course.

swallowed.why: The water cannot sink into the lava.

sidetracked.why: The water has no way out, so it was not diverted into a new course.

worlds.passage: About nine thousand years ago, a tongue of lava poured into a narrow mountain valley and hardened across the floor where a river had wound in wide loops toward a lake. The lava piled up just downstream of a low gap in the valley's western wall, and below the flow the old channel to the lake is dry and grown over with pines. Through that gap a river of the same volume now winds in wide loops down the neighboring valley, where it is the largest stream, and the old lake is fed only by snowmelt. Mapping the valley today, geologists conclude that the lava ______ the river.
worlds.explanation: The old channel is dry, and a river of the same volume now runs through the gap into the next valley, so the river was sent off its course: the lava "sidetracked" it. "Straightened" fails because it still winds in wide loops; "swallowed" fails because it flows through the gap and down the neighboring valley; "trapped" fails because its full volume still flows on.

straightened.why: The river kept its winding form.

swallowed.why: The river still flows on the surface, in a new valley, so it did not vanish into the rock.

trapped.quote: a river of the same volume now winds
trapped.why: The full flow escapes, so it is not held back.

prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In her field guide, one botanist describes these crusts as a living ______.

worlds.passage: Farmers in one northern valley once built hundreds of dry stone walls, and today the walls are coated with lichens, slow-growing crusts of fungus and algae. A pale green species grows thickly on the walls along the old smelter road. In the 1970s, when the smelter ran at full output, its patches bleached and died back every spring a few weeks before the valley's apple trees showed scorched leaves, and families along the road learned to close their windows as soon as the green turned white. In her field guide, one botanist describes these crusts as a living ______.
worlds.explanation: The crusts react to the smelter's fumes weeks before the orchards do, and people act on that signal, so they give early warning: a living "sentinel." "Timeline" fails because patches that die back every spring cannot record steady time; "vestige" fails because the species grows thickly and is no dwindling remnant; "scaffold" fails because the passage describes the crusts warning people, not supporting other plants.

timeline.why: Crusts that shrink back each year do not accumulate a record of elapsed time.

vestige.why: A thriving species is not the surviving trace of something mostly gone.

scaffold.why: Their value lies in the warning people read from them; nothing grows on or from them.

worlds.passage: Farmers in one northern valley once built hundreds of dry stone walls, and today the walls are coated with lichens, slow-growing crusts of fungus and algae. Each crust begins as a speck when a stone is first set and widens in a ring at a pace that hardly varies from decade to decade. Walls that the parish books date to 1760 carry crusts nearly twice as wide as those on walls dated to 1880, and surveyors now measure the widest crust to fix the age of walls the books never mention. In her field guide, one botanist describes these crusts as a living ______.
worlds.explanation: Because each crust starts when the stone is set and widens at a steady pace, its width records how long the wall has stood: a living "timeline." "Sentinel" fails because growth that hardly varies is no signal of any change; "vestige" fails because each crust begins fresh on a newly set stone; "scaffold" fails because the passage is about measuring the crusts, not plants growing on them.

sentinel.why: Crusts that grow the same way whatever happens give no warning of change.

vestige.quote: begins as a speck when a stone is first set
vestige.why: A crust that starts anew on each stone is not a leftover of something older.

scaffold.quote: measure the widest crust to fix the age
scaffold.why: Their use is as a record of age; nothing is said to grow on them.

worlds.passage: Farmers in one northern valley once built hundreds of dry stone walls, and today the walls are coated with lichens, slow-growing crusts of fungus and algae. The commonest crust on the walls is a species otherwise known only from bark in the oak forest that covered the valley until it was cleared four centuries ago. It has never spread to new stone, growing only on walls built from boulders hauled out of that forest's floor, and each decade a few more of its old patches flake away without being replaced. In her field guide, one botanist describes these crusts as a living ______.
worlds.explanation: The crust survives only on stones from a forest that is gone, never spreads, and slowly disappears, so it is a remnant of that vanished forest: a living "vestige." "Sentinel" fails because nothing in its slow loss signals a change in conditions; "timeline" fails because patches that flake away and are never replaced record no steady time; "scaffold" fails because patches that flake off leave nothing for other plants.

sentinel.quote: each decade a few more of its old patches
sentinel.why: A slow, steady loss is not a reaction that warns of anything.

timeline.why: Crusts that are disappearing cannot be read as a record of how long a wall has stood.

scaffold.why: A crust that is only retreating builds nothing for other plants.

worlds.passage: Farmers in one northern valley once built hundreds of dry stone walls, and today the walls are coated with lichens, slow-growing crusts of fungus and algae. Where a crust has covered the top of a wall for a century, the stone beneath it is soft and pitted, and blown dust collects in the crust's folds. On the oldest walls that mix has become a thin dark soil where mosses root first and ferns and small birches follow, while walls scraped clean of their crusts in a 1900 tidying campaign still stand bare. In her field guide, one botanist describes these crusts as a living ______.
worlds.explanation: The crusts break down the stone and gather dust into soil, and only walls that kept them now carry mosses, ferns and birches: a living "scaffold." "Sentinel" fails because the crusts are described building soil, not warning of anything; "timeline" fails because their value is what grows from them, not their size; "vestige" fails because they are the start of a new community, not the remains of an old one.

sentinel.quote: blown dust collects in the crust's folds
sentinel.why: The crusts are described as slowly building soil, not as reacting to conditions.

timeline.quote: mosses root first and ferns and small birches follow
timeline.why: What matters is what grows from them, not any record of time.

vestige.quote: walls scraped clean of their crusts
vestige.why: The crusts begin new plant life rather than surviving from a vanished one.

prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Looking back over seventy years of those surveys, one glaciologist described the glacier's loss of ice as ______.

worlds.passage: Since 1950, survey crews have returned every summer to an eight-kilometer mountain glacier whose lower end lies under a thick blanket of fallen rock. In most years the crews' stakes show the surface within a few centimeters of where it stood the summer before. In three summers, 1962, 1988, and 2011, warm rain fell on the ice for weeks and the front broke into the valley in slabs the size of houses, and those three summers account for nearly all of the two kilometers the front has retreated. Looking back over seventy years of those surveys, one glaciologist described the glacier's loss of ice as ______.
worlds.explanation: Almost all the loss came in three summers decades apart, with little change in between, so it was "sporadic." "Short-lived" fails because the front has retreated two kilometers and stayed back; "slight" fails because two kilometers is a quarter of the glacier; "stealthy" fails because house-sized slabs broke off in plain view.

short-lived.quote: two kilometers the front has retreated
short-lived.why: The front is still back, so the loss has not been undone.

slight.quote: nearly all of the two kilometers
slight.why: Two kilometers of an eight-kilometer glacier is a large loss.

stealthy.why: Loss by collapse in house-sized slabs was in plain sight.

worlds.passage: Since 1950, survey crews have returned every summer to an eight-kilometer mountain glacier whose lower end lies under a thick blanket of fallen rock. Through the warm 1950s the front pulled back a little farther each summer, a full kilometer in all, leaving a strip of raw gravel. A run of snowy winters began in 1959, and the front pushed forward over that same gravel, flattening the young willows that had sprouted there; since 1966 its position has not shifted by more than a few meters. Looking back over seventy years of those surveys, one glaciologist described the glacier's loss of ice as ______.
worlds.explanation: The glacier lost ice through the 1950s, then advanced back over the ground it had lost and has stayed there since 1966, so the loss was "short-lived." "Sporadic" fails because the front pulled back a little each summer; "slight" fails because it lost a full kilometer; "stealthy" fails because the retreat left raw gravel in plain view.

sporadic.why: Loss that came every year was not in scattered bursts.

slight.why: A kilometer of retreat is a large loss.

stealthy.quote: leaving a strip of raw gravel
stealthy.why: The retreat exposed open ground anyone could see.

worlds.passage: Since 1950, survey crews have returned every summer to an eight-kilometer mountain glacier whose lower end lies under a thick blanket of fallen rock. The boulder the first crew painted at the edge of the front in 1950 now sits a short stroll from the ice, and radar shows the ice behind it nearly as thick as on the 1950 maps. Neighboring glaciers have lost a kilometer or more since then; this one, shaded by a high ridge and fed by heavy snow, has changed only by inches a year. Looking back over seventy years of those surveys, one glaciologist described the glacier's loss of ice as ______.
worlds.explanation: The front has moved only a short stroll from a 1950 marker, the ice is nearly as thick as before, and the change came by inches a year, so the loss was "slight." "Sporadic" fails because it came steadily by inches a year; "short-lived" fails because the ice has not returned to the boulder; "stealthy" fails because radar shows the hidden ice is nearly as thick as ever.

sporadic.why: Loss spread evenly over every year was not in scattered bursts.

short-lived.quote: now sits a short stroll from the ice
short-lived.why: The ice has not come back to the 1950 marker, so the loss has not been undone.

stealthy.quote: nearly as thick as on the 1950 maps
stealthy.why: No large loss is hidden beneath the rock.

worlds.passage: Since 1950, survey crews have returned every summer to an eight-kilometer mountain glacier whose lower end lies under a thick blanket of fallen rock. In every summer's photographs the rock-covered front rests against the same boulder it touched in 1950, and early surveyors listed this glacier as one of the few in the range holding steady. Radar soundings begun in 1995 found the ice under the rock sixty meters thinner than the 1950 maps show, and each year's sounding since has found it thinner by about the same amount. Looking back over seventy years of those surveys, one glaciologist described the glacier's loss of ice as ______.
worlds.explanation: The photographs show no change, so surveyors thought the glacier was holding steady, while radar found sixty meters of thinning under the rock: the loss was "stealthy." "Sporadic" fails because it continues by about the same amount each year; "short-lived" fails because the thinning is still going on; "slight" fails because sixty meters is a large loss.

sporadic.why: A steady yearly loss was not in scattered bursts.

short-lived.quote: each year's sounding since has found it thinner
short-lived.why: Loss that continues to the present has not been undone.

slight.why: Sixty meters of thinning is a large loss.

worlds.passage: Each autumn several thousand snow geese fly some three thousand kilometers from the northern tundra to coastal marshes, and ordinarily the whole population lifts off within a few days of one another in mid-October. That year the storms came one after another, and the geese flew only in the calm gaps between them, a few flocks at a time. In her account of one season, an ornithologist wrote that a string of early storms had ______ the geese's migration.

"Truncated" fails because the birds reached the marshes; "spurred" fails because some were still leaving in late November, later than usual; "swelled" fails because the total was roughly the usual one.

spurred.quote: still leaving the tundra in late November

worlds.passage: Each autumn several thousand snow geese fly some three thousand kilometers from the northern tundra to coastal marshes, and ordinarily the whole population lifts off within a few days of one another in mid-October. topic_tag: early measurements of heat from the ocean floor
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Few geologists read the reports when they appeared, and ideas about the ocean floor went on as before for another twenty years. Every heat survey since 1960 has opened by re-measuring the two original sites, and an instrument whose readings there differ from the 1930s values by more than a few percent is sent back for repair. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: Every later survey checks its instruments against the 1930s values, so the measurements serve as the field's standard of comparison: "touchstones." "Watersheds" fails because ideas went on as before for twenty years; "sideshows" fails because every survey since 1960 begins with them; "setbacks" fails because their values are trusted enough to judge instruments by.

watersheds.quote: went on as before for another twenty years
watersheds.why: Measurements after which nothing changed were not turning points.

sideshows.quote: Every heat survey since 1960 has opened
sideshows.why: Work every later survey starts from is central, not peripheral.

setbacks.why: Values used to judge whether instruments work are trusted, not ones that misled the field.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Their readings showed several times more heat escaping than the textbooks allowed for a cold, unchanging seabed. Within ten years those textbooks had been rewritten around a restless ocean floor, though later instruments soon found the 1930s numbers too crude to reuse, and no modern survey refers to them. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: Within ten years the readings had led to rewritten textbooks, so they marked a turning point: "watersheds." "Touchstones" fails because the numbers were too crude to reuse and no survey refers to them; "sideshows" fails because they changed the field's textbooks; "setbacks" fails because they moved the field toward its present view.

touchstones.why: Numbers no one reuses are not standards of comparison.

sideshows.why: Work that changed the textbooks was not peripheral.

setbacks.quote: rewritten around a restless ocean floor
setbacks.why: Readings that moved the field to a new view advanced it rather than holding it back.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Their readings, which later surveys matched almost exactly, appeared in a small regional journal while the field was consumed by an argument over drifting continents. Neither team followed up, and when ocean-floor heat became a central question in the 1960s, the researchers who took it up came across the old papers in a library only after publishing their own results. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: The readings were ignored while the field argued about something else and were found only after the later work was done, so they stood off to the side of the field's story: "sideshows." "Touchstones" fails because the 1960s researchers did not use them; "watersheds" fails because they changed nothing; "setbacks" fails because their values were right and misled no one.

touchstones.quote: only after publishing their own results
touchstones.why: Measurements found after the work was done were not used as a standard.

watersheds.why: Work that went unfollowed was not a turning point.

setbacks.why: Correct values did not lead the field astray.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Heat leaking up along the drill pipes made both readings about ten times too low, and the low numbers seemed to confirm what most geologists already believed, that the ocean floor was cold and inert. For three decades, grant committees cited them when turning down proposals to study the seabed's heat, until a 1962 survey found the leak. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: Wrong readings confirmed a mistaken view and were used for thirty years to block research, so they held the field back: "setbacks." "Touchstones" fails because values ten times too low are no standard; "watersheds" fails because they confirmed the existing view rather than changing it; "sideshows" fails because they shaped funding decisions for three decades.

touchstones.why: Badly wrong values cannot serve as a standard of comparison.

watersheds.why: Measurements that confirmed the existing view did not mark a turning point.

sideshows.why: Measurements that decided what research was funded were not peripheral.

prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: After studying the telescope's record of the event, one astronomer described the dimming as ______.

worlds.passage: In 2019 an orbiting telescope that tracks the brightness of thousands of stars recorded a drop in the light of one star that had shone steadily for years. The star fell to half its usual brightness within an hour, and by the next evening it was shining at its old level again. In the five years since, the telescope has checked it every thirty minutes without once catching it dim, even slightly, a second time. After studying the telescope's record of the event, one astronomer described the dimming as ______.
worlds.explanation: The dimming came and went within about a day and has never recurred in five years of close watching, so it was "transient." "Shallow" fails because the star fell to half its brightness; "stepwise" fails because it fell in one plunge within an hour; "symmetric" fails because the fall took an hour while the recovery took until the next evening.

shallow.why: Losing half its light is a deep drop.

stepwise.why: A single plunge did not come in a series of stages.
